passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id2515454">Have you ever used the Pythagorean Theorem and gotten a wrong answer? passages.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id2515454">Mathematics can begin with a small set of basic assumptions, called <term>postulates</term> or <term>axioms</term>, from which other results follow by logical reasoning. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id3039714">Einstein essentially did the theoretical aspect of this method for <term>relativity</term>. passages.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1331972">The second postulate of special relativity deals with the speed of light. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id2762533">There was a contradiction between this prediction and Newton’s laws, in which velocities add like simple vectors. passages.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id2762533">Applying this prediction in every inertial frame contradicts the intuitive results that come from our experience with classical relativity. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1558765">In the photoelectric effect, we have seen that light, classically understood as waves, behaves like particles sometimes. In 1923 a French physics graduate student named Prince Louis-Victor de Broglie (1892–1987) made a radical proposal based on the hope that nature is symmetric, suggesting that not only EM radiation has both particle and wave properties but that this dual-nature might be universal to all particles. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738257444">The first method is illustrated in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738193776" />. passages.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738257444">The first method is illustrated in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738193776" />. An electron accelerated through a sufficiently large voltage strikes a metal target, such as copper, and ejects an inner-shell electron—one relatively close to and tightly bound to the nucleus—from one of its atoms. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738013737">The second method by which an energetic electron creates an X-ray when it strikes a material is illustrated in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737755554" />. passages.proposed_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" id="import-auto-id1169738013737">In the second method, energetic electrons entering a material are deflected by the electric fields of atomic nuclei. passages.before_xml: <para xmlns="http://cnx.rice.edu/cnxml" xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="import-auto-id1514494">Two types of experimental evidence imply that Becquerel’s rays originate not from the atomic structure, but something smaller inside. First, the radiation is found to be associated with certain elements, such as uranium. Radiation does not vary with chemical state—that is, uranium is radioactive whether it is in the form of an element or compound. In addition, radiation does not vary with temperature, pressure, or ionization state of the uranium atom. Since all of these factors affect electrons in an atom, the radiation cannot come from electron transitions, as atomic spectra do. The huge energy emitted during each event is the second piece of evidence that the radiation cannot be atomic in origin. Nuclear radiation has energies of the order of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>6</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em" /><m:mtext>eV</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"10" rSup { size 8{6} } "eV"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> per event, which is much greater than the typical atomic energies (a few <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mtext>eV</m:mtext></m:mrow><m:mrow /></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"eV"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>), such as that observed in spectra and chemical reactions, and more than ten times as high as the most energetic characteristic X-rays. Becquerel did not vigorously pursue his discovery for very long. In 1898, Marie Curie (1867–1934) began her doctoral study of Becquerel’s rays. She and her husband—French physicist Pierre Curie (1859–1906)—soon discovered two new radioactive elements, which she named <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">polonium</emphasis></emphasis> (after her native land) and <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">radium</emphasis></emphasis> (because it radiates). These two new elements filled holes in the periodic table and, further, displayed much higher levels of radioactivity per gram of material than uranium. Over a period of four years, working under poor conditions and spending their own funds, the Curies processed more than a ton of uranium ore to isolate a gram of radium salt.
